proposalSnapshot.speaker: William Lane Craig
proposalSnapshot.proposition: Because the universe began to exist, it has a transcendent cause whose relation to time, space, and the causal regress requires it to be uncaused, timeless, changeless, spaceless, and immaterial.
proposalSnapshot.attributionBasis: The fixed source span was resolved in the prior two-vote source stage; the complete transcript and surrounding context identify William Lane Craig as the continuous speaker.
proposalSnapshot.rationale: This is Craig's principal Kalam inference from a finite beginning to an uncaused, timeless, spaceless, immaterial transcendent cause and is necessary to represent the pro cosmological route.

proposalSnapshot.speaker: William Lane Craig
proposalSnapshot.proposition: The constants and initial quantities occupy an extraordinarily narrow life-permitting range and match an independently specified pattern, so physical necessity and chance are inadequate and design is the best explanation.
proposalSnapshot.attributionBasis: Craig is the formally introduced opening speaker from event 79 through event 510, and this uninterrupted numbered fine-tuning argument follows his explicit transition at events 258-259.
proposalSnapshot.rationale: This is the missing constructive statement of the accepted pro fine-tuning bridge.

proposalSnapshot.speaker: William Lane Craig
proposalSnapshot.proposition: Atheistic evolution and social conditioning do not make morality objectively binding, while moral experience defeasibly reveals objective values; therefore God exists as their necessary ground.
proposalSnapshot.attributionBasis: The span remains within Craig's uninterrupted opening speech and follows his numbered transition to the moral argument at event 324.
proposalSnapshot.rationale: Craig's moral argument is one of his five expressly cumulative evidential lines and is absent from the seeds.

proposalSnapshot.speaker: William Lane Craig
proposalSnapshot.proposition: Jesus' empty tomb, post-mortem appearances, and the disciples' unexpected resurrection belief lack a plausible naturalistic explanation and are best explained by God raising Jesus, thereby evidencing God's existence.
proposalSnapshot.attributionBasis: The span is within Craig's uninterrupted opening and begins at the resurrection claim after his numbered transition to Jesus at event 407.
proposalSnapshot.rationale: This supplies the missing constructive argument for the accepted pro resurrection bridge.

proposalSnapshot.speaker: William Lane Craig
proposalSnapshot.proposition: A sincere seeker can know that God exists apart from argument through immediate personal experience, in which God is encountered as a directly given reality rather than merely adopted as an idea.
proposalSnapshot.attributionBasis: Craig explicitly marks this as his fifth point at event 473 and continues without a speaker change through event 500.
proposalSnapshot.rationale: Personal religious experience is one of Craig's five cumulative evidential lines and must be represented for motion-level coverage.

proposalSnapshot.speaker: Peter Millican
proposalSnapshot.proposition: Because mutually incompatible religions are acquired and maintained through similar sources such as upbringing, preaching, sacred texts, and religious experience, those methods are unreliable guides to truth.
proposalSnapshot.attributionBasis: Millican is the formally introduced speaker from event 519 through event 1051; the span is an uninterrupted portion of his opening case and explicitly distinguishes this argument from a genetic fallacy.
proposalSnapshot.rationale: This is Millican's direct reliability objection to Craig's appeal to personal religious experience and is more assessment-relevant than the excluded historical-science seed.

proposalSnapshot.speaker: Peter Millican
proposalSnapshot.proposition: Even generously allowing disembodied mentality some prior probability, the specific omniperfect Christian God must compete with thousands of conflicting religious hypotheses, so absent an overwhelmingly strong case the rational conclusion is disbelief or at least agnosticism.
proposalSnapshot.attributionBasis: The span is within Millican's uninterrupted opening speech and follows his explicit burden-of-proof discussion at events 712-765.
proposalSnapshot.rationale: This states the con route's motion-level specificity and comparative-burden thesis.

proposalSnapshot.speaker: Peter Millican
proposalSnapshot.proposition: Ordinary causal experience concerns rearrangements of existing material and therefore does not justify extending the premise that whatever begins to exist has a cause to creation from nothing.
proposalSnapshot.attributionBasis: The fixed source span was resolved in the prior two-vote source stage; the complete transcript and surrounding context identify Peter Millican as the continuous speaker.
proposalSnapshot.rationale: Millican directly attacks the Kalam causal premise by distinguishing experienced material rearrangement from creation ex nihilo.

proposalSnapshot.speaker: Peter Millican
proposalSnapshot.proposition: The Borde-Guth-Vilenkin theorem establishes only a beginning to expansion under its assumptions, permits prior contraction models, and cannot warrant confidence about the global universe where relativity and quantum mechanics break down.
proposalSnapshot.attributionBasis: Millican remains the uninterrupted opening speaker and explicitly turns to Craig's physical case for the universe's beginning at event 902.
proposalSnapshot.rationale: Candidate 03 addresses causation but not Craig's separate scientific premise that the universe began; this move supplies that major missing reply.

proposalSnapshot.speaker: Peter Millican
proposalSnapshot.proposition: There is no evidence that minds exist without physical substrates, and even if the universe had a nonphysical cause it need not be an abstract object or mind but could be a kind of cause beyond evolved human comprehension.
proposalSnapshot.attributionBasis: This is the next uninterrupted portion of Millican's opening response to the Kalam argument, introduced by his transition at event 969.
proposalSnapshot.rationale: This directly attacks the step from a transcendent cause to a personal unembodied mind, a central specificity issue not captured by seed 03.

proposalSnapshot.speaker: William Lane Craig
proposalSnapshot.proposition: Religious disagreement does not discredit one common belief-forming method because religions do not share a single method, while Craig's own case uses logic, evidence, and personal experience.
proposalSnapshot.attributionBasis: The fixed source span was resolved in the prior two-vote source stage; the complete transcript and surrounding context identify William Lane Craig as the continuous speaker.
proposalSnapshot.rationale: Craig directly answers Millican's religious-diversity challenge by denying a single common religious method and identifying his own method as logic, evidence, and experience.

proposalSnapshot.speaker: William Lane Craig
proposalSnapshot.proposition: The Borde-Guth-Vilenkin theorem still implies an absolute cosmic beginning, is independent of Einstein's gravitational equations and any quantum-gravity description, and therefore supplies strong cosmological evidence that the universe began.
proposalSnapshot.attributionBasis: Craig is introduced for rebuttal at events 1060-1063 and speaks uninterrupted here while explicitly answering Millican's BGV objections.
proposalSnapshot.rationale: This is Craig's principal technical answer to Millican's attack on the scientific beginning premise.

proposalSnapshot.speaker: William Lane Craig
proposalSnapshot.proposition: The absence of observed creation from nothing does not undermine causation, because originating without either material or efficient cause would be still more absurd than originating without a material cause alone.
proposalSnapshot.attributionBasis: The span continues Craig's uninterrupted rebuttal and begins with his explicit attribution of the objection to Millican at event 1235.
proposalSnapshot.rationale: This directly answers the seed's material-rearrangement objection to the Kalam causal premise.

proposalSnapshot.speaker: Peter Millican
proposalSnapshot.proposition: If the fundamental constants were shown to be physically inexplicable and precisely selected from a broad range of alternatives, that coincidence would naturally invite explanation by a cosmic designer.
proposalSnapshot.attributionBasis: Millican is introduced for this rebuttal at events 1368-1371 and explicitly says he concedes this much at event 1385 within an uninterrupted turn.
proposalSnapshot.rationale: This explicit conditional concession materially acknowledges the potential evidential force of Craig's fine-tuning argument while preserving Millican's subsequent doubts about whether its conditions are met.

proposalSnapshot.speaker: Peter Millican
proposalSnapshot.proposition: Fine-tuning warrants caution because humans readily over-detect purpose, cosmic probability judgments rest on one observed universe, deeper physics may explain the constants, and a multiverse would make life-permitting observation unsurprising.
proposalSnapshot.attributionBasis: The fixed source span was resolved in the prior two-vote source stage; the complete transcript and surrounding context identify Peter Millican as the continuous speaker.
proposalSnapshot.rationale: This is Millican's main probability, future-physics, and multiverse undercutter of Craig's fine-tuning inference.

proposalSnapshot.speaker: Peter Millican
proposalSnapshot.proposition: Even established cosmic fine-tuning would not identify the morally perfect Christian God because the same life-enabling conditions are equally compatible with an evil or morally neutral designer.
proposalSnapshot.attributionBasis: The span is within Millican's uninterrupted fine-tuning rebuttal and is introduced as a distinct objection at event 1457.
proposalSnapshot.rationale: Seed 05 captures probability and multiverse objections but not the separate failure of fine-tuning to identify the Christian God's moral character.

proposalSnapshot.speaker: Peter Millican
proposalSnapshot.proposition: The nonunique result of subtracting infinity from infinity is not a contradiction but merely reflects that the inverse equation has multiple solutions, just as division of zero by zero is undefined without making zero incoherent.
proposalSnapshot.attributionBasis: Millican remains the uninterrupted rebuttal speaker and expressly develops his response to Craig's actual-infinity argument in this span.
proposalSnapshot.rationale: This directly contests Craig's philosophical argument that actual infinities are impossible, a distinct premise not addressed by seed 03.

proposalSnapshot.speaker: Peter Millican
proposalSnapshot.proposition: Although absence of evidence is not always evidence of absence, a perfect God should make his existence substantially more plausible than that of an anti-God, whereas the observed world does not do so.
proposalSnapshot.attributionBasis: This remains within Millican's uninterrupted rebuttal and explicitly answers Craig's preceding absence-of-evidence argument before returning to cosmology.
proposalSnapshot.rationale: This supplies the hiddenness and comparative-expectation claim to which seed 06 directly responds and supports the con empirical route.

proposalSnapshot.speaker: William Lane Craig
proposalSnapshot.proposition: Absence of evidence counts against God only if God's existence would make substantially more evidence probable, and Millican has supplied no grounds for that expectation beyond personal opinion.
proposalSnapshot.attributionBasis: The fixed source span was resolved in the prior two-vote source stage; the complete transcript and surrounding context identify William Lane Craig as the continuous speaker.
proposalSnapshot.rationale: Craig directly disputes the evidential-hiddenness premise that substantially greater evidence should be expected if God existed.

proposalSnapshot.speaker: William Lane Craig
proposalSnapshot.proposition: Millican's admission that infinite subtraction lacks a unique value is precisely the problem for a real collection, because physically removing equal infinite quantities from equal totals should not yield unequal remainders.
proposalSnapshot.attributionBasis: Craig begins this uninterrupted rebuttal at event 1701 and explicitly turns to Millican's infinity response at event 1751.
proposalSnapshot.rationale: This is Craig's substantive answer to Millican's mathematical defense of actual infinity.

proposalSnapshot.speaker: William Lane Craig
proposalSnapshot.proposition: Fine-tuning probabilities can be assessed by comparing possible parameter ranges with the narrow life-permitting range, diverse cases are unlikely all to disappear under future physics, and moral character is supplied by Craig's separate moral argument.
proposalSnapshot.attributionBasis: Craig remains the uninterrupted rebuttal speaker and explicitly enumerates answers to Millican's fine-tuning objections in this span.
proposalSnapshot.rationale: This captures Craig's main response to both Millican's probabilistic uncertainty and the objection that fine-tuning alone does not establish goodness.

proposalSnapshot.speaker: Peter Millican
proposalSnapshot.proposition: An atheist can apprehend a moral value without knowing its ultimate nature, just as one can perceive a physical object, and God's existence makes no evident difference to that apprehension or to belief in objective values.
proposalSnapshot.attributionBasis: Millican is introduced for his final rebuttal at events 1920-1923 and continues uninterrupted through this focused response to Craig's moral-perception analogy.
proposalSnapshot.rationale: This directly attacks Craig's claim that objective moral value and its apprehension require God.

proposalSnapshot.speaker: Peter Millican
proposalSnapshot.proposition: The resurrection reports are late, non-eyewitness Christian advocacy documents; Matthew and Luke depend on Mark and another common source, and the accounts contain chronological and theological discrepancies, so they provide weak evidence for God.
proposalSnapshot.attributionBasis: The span remains within Millican's uninterrupted final rebuttal and begins with his explicit transition to the resurrection at event 2048.
proposalSnapshot.rationale: This is Millican's principal source-critical reply to Craig's resurrection case.

proposalSnapshot.speaker: William Lane Craig
proposalSnapshot.proposition: Human rationality supplies no nonarbitrary basis for intrinsic moral value on atheism, and objective moral obligations and prohibitions are especially unintelligible without a moral lawgiver.
proposalSnapshot.attributionBasis: Craig is introduced for closing remarks at events 2122-2125 and speaks uninterrupted here while explicitly returning to Millican's moral objections.
proposalSnapshot.rationale: This is Craig's closing answer to Millican's proposed non-theistic grounding of objective value and obligation.

proposalSnapshot.speaker: William Lane Craig
proposalSnapshot.proposition: The three facts used in Craig's resurrection inference are accepted by a majority of historians, and even Millican's cited skeptical scholars accept the empty tomb, appearances, and origin of the disciples' belief.
proposalSnapshot.attributionBasis: Craig remains the uninterrupted closing speaker and explicitly turns to Millican's Gospel-discrepancy objection at event 2214.
proposalSnapshot.rationale: This directly answers Millican's source-critical attack by distinguishing disputed Gospel details from Craig's claimed historical core.

proposalSnapshot.speaker: Peter Millican
proposalSnapshot.proposition: The observed world's evil and purported divine morality do not match expectations for a perfect God, so the evidence favors skepticism and provides strong evidence against God's existence with very little in favor.
proposalSnapshot.attributionBasis: The fixed source span was resolved in the prior two-vote source stage; the complete transcript and surrounding context identify Peter Millican as the continuous speaker.
proposalSnapshot.rationale: Millican states the con route's principal positive empirical case: the world's evil and attributed divine morality are less expected under a perfect God than under skepticism.

proposalSnapshot.speaker: William Lane Craig
proposalSnapshot.proposition: Fine-tuning and Craig's other presented arguments do not establish infinite power; at most they infer a being of enormous power, while an additional ontological argument would be needed for infinity.
proposalSnapshot.attributionBasis: In the moderated exchange, Millican finishes at event 2792 with an address to Bill, and Craig immediately answers in events 2793-2800 before Millican resumes at event 2801.
proposalSnapshot.rationale: This explicitly and materially narrows what Craig claims his presented evidential arguments establish about the specifically omnipotent Christian God.

proposalSnapshot.speaker: William Lane Craig
proposalSnapshot.proposition: Natural and moral evil may be permitted because God's purpose is to bring people freely into an eternal relationship with him, and an evil-containing world may maximize those who freely do so.
proposalSnapshot.attributionBasis: The fixed source span was resolved in the prior two-vote source stage; the complete transcript and surrounding context identify William Lane Craig as the continuous speaker.
proposalSnapshot.rationale: Craig supplies his principal purpose-based response to the empirical problem of evil, proposing that an evil-containing world may maximize freely formed relationships with God.

proposalBridgeCoverage.rationale: Craig's five selected constructive lines collectively supply his stated cumulative evidential case for Christian theism over skeptical atheism.
The five constructive evidential lines and Craig's selected replies to religious disagreement, hiddenness, and evil represent the cumulative convergence and his denial of a comparable atheistic case.
Craig's Kalam construction and his replies concerning BGV, causation, and actual infinity represent the finite-beginning and transcendent-cause bridge.
Craig's design inference and his answer to probability, future-physics, and specificity objections represent the pro fine-tuning bridge.
Craig's three-fact resurrection argument and his defense of its historical core represent the accepted resurrection bridge.
Millican's specificity and burden thesis, comparative hiddenness claim, and empirical argument from evil directly support withholding or rejecting belief in the Christian God.

The selected moves represent Millican's central underdetermination case across religious experience, cosmology, fine-tuning, morality, and resurrection, together with the burden imposed by the hypothesis's specificity.
Millican attacks the causal generalization from ordinary experience, the scientific beginning premise, and the philosophical rejection of actual infinity.
Millican's probability, deeper-physics, multiverse, and designer-specificity objections represent the accepted con fine-tuning bridge.
Millican's arguments from the world's evil, attributed divine morality, and insufficiently discriminating divine evidence represent the contrary empirical-expectation bridge.

proposalConcessionAudit.rationale: Craig materially concedes that the arguments presented establish at most enormous rather than infinite power and would require a further argument for omnipotence.
Millican materially concedes that genuinely inexplicable precise fine-tuning would naturally invite a cosmic-designer explanation, while disputing whether the antecedent is established.
